accuracy.evidence: Definitions follow early-years maths usage: a pair is two items that are the same; matching compares attributes (colour, shape, size, pattern) and is the precursor to sorting by attribute and to one-to-one correspondence. Development Matters (2023) lists comparing sizes and noticing patterns under Mathematics for birth to three and three and four year olds, and NCETM early-years guidance places matching before sorting and counting. Every lab outcome is consistent: only same-colour AND same-pattern socks pair, lids fit only the same-size pot, and the lonely item is the only one appearing once.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented toddler slip of matching on one salient feature: the red stripy decoy sock tempts a colour-only match and gets 'Both are red, but one has stripes and one has spots'; the big duck / little duck and red circle / red square rounds tempt 'same kind = same'; lids that are too big or too small target ignoring size; the challenge uses near-misses (tiger for cat, green apple, tomato, blue car, stripy fish).

lab_distinct.evidence: Built around this topic's own action of pairing identical objects: a washing line where loose socks are dragged beside their partner, a turn-over-two-cards pairs game, a same / not-the-same judgement, an odd-one-with-no-pair finder and size-matched lids on pots. No other flagship has a pairs memory game or a washing-line pairing; the shingle gate passed against all flag_*.js files.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child first discovers that colour alone is not enough (decoy sock), then practises spotting identical pictures, then names same versus not the same across size, shape and colour, then uses the pair idea in reverse (which one has no pair), then extends matching to size with lids. This mirrors the topic evidence: matches pairs of socks, plays a picture matching game, says 'same' about a pair.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option: 'red stripy sock' for the red spotty sock (colour-only match, disproved when it will not hang), 'Same' for a big and a little duck (disproved by the size feedback), and 'the little lid' for the big pot (disproved when the little lid falls in).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating find-the-same questions with ten distinct m= messages naming the slip: tiger (stripes but bigger), dog (animal but not a cat), green apple (same shape, wrong colour), tomato (red and round but not an apple), blue car, bus, sock vs glove, shoe vs glove, stripy fish, whale.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are 2-8 word read-aloud sentences with concrete objects (socks, gloves, ducks) under the family kid FK limit; canvas headings are one short line; every button is one to three words plus an emoji. Adult text names the EYFS area and the terms attribute, sorting and one-to-one correspondence within the adult limit.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and 12% duplicate gate. Kid text covers what a pair is, what to look at, two near-miss examples and how to say how things match; adult text covers curriculum placement, the one-feature slip, the language to model and what the lab does. Each lab step has its own job.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots of all six steps before and after Show me in light and dark: the first shots showed socks drawn as tiny pills (a path bug) and they were redrawn larger as proper sock shapes; the six cards fill a 3x2 grid, the two compared items sit side by side, five lonely-row items fit in one row, three pots and lids fit, and the challenge emoji buttons fit one row. Buttons use the young-learner 56 px size.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes and there are no console errors. Every drag has a button route (sock buttons naming colour and pattern, Card 1-6 buttons, Same / Not the same, labelled emoji buttons for the lonely row and challenge, lid-to-pot buttons) and the canvas aria-label says what happened after each move.
